faqs.question: How many items should go in a Halloween party favor bag?
faqs.answer: Two to four is enough for most children's parties: one toy they will actually use, one or two small extras and an optional treat. More items usually means cheaper ones that break before the car ride home.

faqs.question: How much should I spend on Halloween favors per child?
faqs.answer: Our estimates put a decent paper-and-toy bag at about $2, a fuller one at about $5 and a keepsake bag with a tote at about $10 per guest at 10 guests. Buying for 25 guests usually lowers the unit price because multipacks get cheaper per piece.

faqs.question: What are good non-candy fillers for Halloween party bags?
faqs.answer: Kazoos, temporary tattoos, mini notepads, origami paper, riddle cards, modelling dough and seed packets all work. Keep them in a separate bowl or bag, the way the Teal Pumpkin Project suggests, so children with food allergies can choose freely.

faqs.question: What can I put in a Halloween favor bag for a 2-year-old?
faqs.answer: Stick to things too big to swallow: a board book, a whole mini pumpkin with the stem removed, a cotton bib or jumbo crayons you have size-checked yourself. Skip balloons, spider rings, marbles, hard candies and anything that smells like food.

faqs.question: Do adults expect favors at a Halloween party?
faqs.answer: No, but a small consumable one is a nice close to the night. A seed packet, a single-serve coffee bag or a jar of homemade spice rub costs about $1 to $1.50 each and leaves nothing to store.

faqs.question: Is it rude to hand out favor bags with no candy in them?
faqs.answer: Not if the bag has something to play with. In a three-year porch experiment, roughly a quarter of trick-or-treaters chose raisins over chocolate even without a nudge, so plenty of children are happy with a non-candy option.

faqs.question: When should I pack the favor bags?
faqs.answer: One or two days before the party, once your guest count is firm. Packing on the day is when items get missed and toddler bags end up with small parts from an older child's batch.

faqs.question: Are compostable party bags better than plastic ones?
faqs.answer: Only if they actually reach a compost facility, and many guests will not have one. A plain kraft paper bag, or a canvas tote that is itself the favor, is the simpler low-waste choice.

faqs.question: Can I send a thank-you to just one child after the party?
faqs.answer: Yes. SubhSandesh's Halloween page has a kids mode with no gore and no jump scares, and you can add up to six photos and a short letter, then share a private link to open on a parent's phone. It is made for one recipient, so it is not a way to thank a whole guest list.

faqs.question: Which Halloween favors are best for 8 to 12 year olds?
faqs.answer: Pick something with a challenge in it: a riddle-card deck, a 100-piece mini puzzle, origami paper or an invisible-ink pen with a UV light. Children this age lose interest fast in toys meant for preschoolers.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Halloween Party Favors by Age and Budget, Priced Per Guest

The best Halloween party favors match the guest's age first and your budget second: small-part-free items for under-3s, one toy plus an optional treat for ages 4 to 12, and something useful for teens and adults. Plan on roughly $2, $5 or $10 a bag, with at least one non-candy item so a guest with a food allergy is never left out. Below are 32 favors with estimated unit costs at 10 and 25 guests, a choking flag and a sugar-free flag.

SubhSandesh builds greeting pages, not party supplies. Of the 5,199 pages made on the platform since March 2026, 48.3% were opened on a phone, which is why the one digital extra here is a thank-you a child opens on a parent's phone.

## What are Halloween party favors, or party favours and bag fillers?

A Halloween party favor is a small gift each guest takes home, usually 1 to 4 items in a bag or pail. In the UK and Australia it is a party favour or party bag, and the items inside are "party bag fillers".

One toy a child plays with tomorrow beats five that break tonight. That rule shapes every pick below.

## 32 Halloween party favors by age, with unit costs

Prices are our estimates from typical US multipack prices in October, per guest at 10 guests, then at 25. "Choke-safe" means no risk for under-3s; "sugar-free" means no sugar at all.

### 1. Toddlers, under 3: nothing that fits a toilet-paper tube

For this age the test is size. If a favor, or any piece that could snap off, slides through a toilet-paper tube, leave it out.

- **Pumpkin or ghost board book**: $3.50/$2.75; choke-safe; sugar-free
- **Jumbo triangle crayons, 3-pack**: $1.20/$0.90; crayons are exempt from the small-parts rule, so check size yourself; sugar-free
- **Whole mini pumpkin, stem removed**: $1.50/$1.00; choke-safe once the stem is off; sugar-free
- **Cotton bat-print bandana bib**: $2.50/$1.80; choke-safe; sugar-free

### 2. Ages 4 to 7: the same core toy for everyone

Children this age trade favors before leaving, so give everyone the same core item. Keep these bags from toddler siblings.

- **Halloween temporary tattoo sheet**: $0.60/$0.35; risk under 3; sugar-free
- **Felt finger puppet (bat, cat or ghost)**: $1.00/$0.70; risk under 3; sugar-free
- **Paper bat mask to colour**: $0.90/$0.60; choke-safe; sugar-free
- **Plastic spider ring**: $0.15/$0.10; high risk under 3; sugar-free

### 3. Ages 8 to 12: something to do on the way home

Older children judge a favor on whether it is boring. Pick one with a challenge or a secret inside.

- **Pocket riddle-card deck**: $1.20/$0.90; choke-safe; sugar-free
- **Origami paper printed with bats**: $0.80/$0.50; choke-safe; sugar-free
- **Invisible-ink pen with UV light**: $1.50/$1.10; small parts; check the battery door is screwed shut; sugar-free
- **100-piece haunted-house mini puzzle**: $2.00/$1.50; risk under 3; sugar-free

### 4. Teens: useful beats cute

Teenagers keep favors they would have bought themselves. Black and orange beats cartoon ghosts.

- **Black satin scrunchie**: $1.00/$0.70; fine for teens; sugar-free
- **Pocket sketchbook with a skull cover**: $1.50/$1.10; choke-safe; sugar-free
- **Moon-print phone grip**: $2.50/$1.80; fine for teens; sugar-free
- **One printed party-booth photo**: $1.00/$1.00; choke-safe; sugar-free

### 5. Adults: small, consumable, gone in a week

Adult guests do not want a toy to store. Give something they use up, plant or switch on.

- **Pumpkin seed packet with a "grow your own" tag**: $1.50/$1.20; choke-safe; sugar-free
- **LED tea light in a small jar**: $1.20/$0.85; button cell, keep from children; sugar-free
- **Mini jar of homemade "witch's dust" spice rub**: $1.50/$1.10; choke-safe; sugar-free
- **Drip coffee bag labelled "midnight brew"**: $0.90/$0.70; choke-safe; sugar-free

### 6. Non-candy and allergy-friendly favors

FARE, the US food allergy charity behind the Teal Pumpkin Project, keeps a [list of non-food treat ideas](https://www.foodallergy.org/resources/ideas-non-food-treats) and asks that they sit in a bowl apart from any candy. That list also includes spider rings, bouncy balls, erasers and coins, so allergy-safe is not the same as toddler-safe.

- **Orange or black kazoo**: $0.40/$0.30; risk under 3; sugar-free
- **Mini notepad and bat-topper pencil**: $0.90/$0.65; topper is a risk under 3; sugar-free
- **Reflective zip-pull for a coat**: $0.70/$0.50; risk under 3; sugar-free
- **Tub of modelling dough**: $0.80/$0.55; choke-safe; many doughs contain wheat, so read the label; sugar-free

### 7. Eco and zero-waste favors

The greenest favor has no bag at all. These replace the packaging or outlive the party.

- **Canvas tote stamped with a ghost (the bag is the favor)**: $2.00/$1.40; choke-safe; sugar-free
- **Pencil made from recycled newspaper**: $0.50/$0.35; choke-safe; sugar-free
- **Wooden spinning top**: $1.20/$0.90; risk under 3; sugar-free
- **Wildflower seed ball in paper**: $0.60/$0.45; high risk under 3; sugar-free

### 8. DIY favors

Homemade favors cost the least per guest and the most in time. Budget an evening for 25.

- **Clothespin bats with card wings**: $0.30/$0.25; spring is a risk under 3; sugar-free
- **Printed trick-or-treat bingo card**: $0.10/$0.10; choke-safe; sugar-free
- **Paper fortune teller with spooky dares**: $0.05/$0.05; choke-safe; sugar-free
- **Mini box of raisins with a ghost label**: $0.40/$0.30; dried fruit, keep from toddlers; no added sugar, not sugar-free

## Halloween party favor picks by age, side by side

One strong pick per age band, compared on cost and the two safety questions parents ask. Costs are estimates.

| Age | Favor | Est. unit cost (10 / 25 guests) | Choking-safe | Sugar-free |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Under 3 | Pumpkin board book | $3.50 / $2.75 | Yes | Yes |
| 4–7 | Paper bat mask | $0.90 / $0.60 | Yes | Yes |
| 8–12 | Riddle-card deck | $1.20 / $0.90 | Yes | Yes |
| Teens | Pocket sketchbook | $1.50 / $1.10 | Yes | Yes |
| Adults | Pumpkin seed packet | $1.50 / $1.20 | Yes | Yes |

Paper and card favors win every row on cost and safety. Plastic picks are where the choking flags cluster.

## How to build a Halloween favor bag at $2, $5 or $10 per guest

Candy is already the default. The National Retail Federation's [September 2026 Halloween survey](https://nrf.com/media-center/press-releases/nrf-halloween-survey-shows-consumer-spending-expected-to-reach-13-5-billion) found 96% of consumers planned to buy sweets, worth $4.1 billion, within an average spend of $115.14 per person.

So these bags lead with a toy and treat candy as optional. Totals are our estimates at 10 guests.

- **The $2 bag (about $1.80):** paper bat mask, bingo card and fortune teller ($1.05); kraft paper bag with a stamped ghost ($0.40); one optional fun-size treat ($0.35)
- **The $5 bag (about $4.80):** felt finger puppet ($1.00), riddle-card deck ($1.20), temporary tattoos ($0.60), kazoo ($0.40), mini box of raisins ($0.40), kraft bag with a name tag ($0.50) and one optional treat ($0.70)
- **The $10 bag (about $9.50):** canvas ghost tote as the bag ($2.00), mini puzzle ($2.00), invisible-ink pen ($1.50), pocket sketchbook ($1.50), wooden spinning top ($1.20), modelling dough ($0.80) and one optional treat ($0.50)

A "compostable" film bag only beats plastic if it reaches a compost facility, so plain kraft paper is the simpler choice. Pack early, too: in our Raksha Bandhan 2026 data (a different festival, n = 89 pages), 49.4% of pages were built on the day itself, and a bag packed on the day shows it.

## Choking hazards: what the 16 CFR 1500.19 and 1501 small-parts rules cover

In the US, part 1501 bans toys intended for children under 3 years (36 months) if they, or a piece that breaks off, fit inside the federal test cylinder. [16 CFR 1500.19](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-16/chapter-II/subchapter-C/part-1500/section-1500.19) adds a "CHOKING HAZARD" warning on small-part toys for ages 3 to 5, on every latex balloon, and on small balls, meaning ones that pass through a 1.75-inch (44.4 mm) hole. Balloons, paper articles such as books, and writing materials such as crayons and chalk are exempt from the under-3 ban under 16 CFR 1501.3, so "legal" does not mean "safe for a toddler's bag".

A 2023 review of [risk factors and prevention of choking](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC10811631) in the European Journal of Translational Myology lists balloons, marbles, hard candies, buttons and small coins as items to keep from young children. It also warns against objects that smell like food, naming erasers, which is why scented novelty erasers are not on this list.

## Do non-candy favors work? Two studies and one campaign

Yes, when children get the choice. In a [three-year porch experiment with 1,223 trick-or-treaters](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC5749710) published in PLOS ONE in 2018, 23.5% of the comparison group chose a box of raisins over chocolate, rising to 28.1% in the treatment group.

Adults are the bigger obstacle. A 2025 [survey of 256 elementary teachers](https://europepmc.org/article/PMC/PMC12780796) in Public Health Nutrition found 55.9% used candy as a classroom reward at least sometimes, and perceived barriers to stopping predicted it, not policy.

For a host, that means a bowl of non-food favors beside the candy, and letting each child pick. Even the porch study's comparison group took the raisins about one time in four.

## A thank-you page for one child, and when it's the wrong choice

Our [Halloween greeting page](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween) is not a party tool: it greets one person and will not send 25 thank-you notes. It fits the one child you want to thank, such as a niece who stuffed every bag. In kids mode the look is spooky-cute: nothing gory, nothing jumps out, a trick turns into confetti spiders, and the No button just offers "maybe later?".

Your helper knocks on the door three times, carves a pumpkin until the word you picked lights up, and wipes fog off portraits to reveal up to six photos. The finale is a Boo License, a 1080 × 1920 PNG at Instagram Story size, and an email reaches you once they answer. For a grandparent who missed the party, the [premium Halloween page](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween-premium) adds a 60-second voice note and room for 12 photos, and its family and kids modes never show a No button.

Skip both when a thank-you at the door will do. The page's interface is in English, and since 48.3% of shared pages get opened on a phone, a family without one is a poor fit; a handwritten tag on each bag thanks the whole guest list.

## Sources

- National Retail Federation, Halloween consumer survey press release, 22 September 2026.
- eCFR, 16 CFR 1500.19, choking-hazard labelling for small parts, balloons and small balls (current text).
- Saccomanno et al., "Risk factors and prevention of choking", European Journal of Translational Myology, 27 October 2023.
- Aronow, Karlan and Pinson, trick-or-treaters' dietary choices, PLOS ONE, 2 January 2018.
- Daniels et al., "Health Belief Model constructs and teachers' use of food rewards", Public Health Nutrition, 27 October 2025.
- FARE, "Ideas for Non-Food Treats" (undated).

auditReport.honestAssessment: The measured top 10 is weak (7 of 10: two hijacked-subdomain spam pages, a 404, a bot-walled 2017 retailer post, a 2014 affiliate list, a promotional-products blog and a duplicate Punchbowl URL), and none of the readable pages gives a unit cost, a choking flag, an allergy option or a source; this post is the only one with all four, tied to 16 CFR 1501's exemptions and two open-access studies. Its first-party data is only tangential (platform-wide phone-open share and a Raksha Bandhan build-timing analogue), the unit costs are our estimates rather than measured prices, and the domain has little authority on party supplies, so expect slow gains and do not expect it to displace Punchbowl.
